outcome.rationale: Trial likely to meet primary efficacy endpoint showing both treatments reduce extension deficit. Non-inferiority of collagenase expected at 3 months. Long-term durability favors surgery; may show statistically significant difference in secondary recurrence endpoints. Safety profiles acceptable for both. Study adequately powered for primary endpoint but secondary outcomes have higher uncertainty.

primary_rollup.rule: success=全部主要终点yes；fail=任一主要终点no；其余uncertain
primary_rollup.binarize_rule: uncertain 且 P>=0.5 记 yes、P<0.5 记 no 后再聚合（阈值缺失时的兜底口径，非模型原始判断）

value.effect_measure: mean change in total active extension deficit (degrees)
value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline to 3 months, both treatment groups combined and separately
value.uncertainty: No direct evidence from recurrent disease RCTs; extrapolated from primary disease trials. Blinding may be imperfect. Small sample size increases variance.
value.rationale: Both treatments effectively reduce contracture. Fasciectomy typically achieves greater immediate correction; collagenase shows slightly less magnitude but clinically meaningful improvement. Based on DISC trial and meta-analyses of primary disease applied to recurrent population with conservative estimate.

value.estimand: ITT population, proportion with ≥20 degree worsening at 24 months compared to 3 months post-treatment
value.uncertainty: Novel endpoint definition; prior studies report recurrence not worsening threshold. Limited long-term data for recurrent disease. Higher recurrence expected with collagenase.
value.rationale: Worsening threshold of 20 degrees is stringent. Recurrence rates in prior studies suggest 20-40% retreatment rates at 2-5 years for collagenase versus 10-30% for fasciectomy. Predict collagenase group exceeds threshold more frequently.

value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline across all timepoints (3 weeks to 60 months)
value.uncertainty: QuickDASH validated for Dupuytren; expected improvement based on primary disease studies. Recurrent disease may have lower magnitude of improvement due to chronicity.
value.rationale: QuickDASH improvements of 15-25 points typical after successful Dupuytren treatment. Both interventions improve function; surgical group may show slightly greater improvement due to more complete contracture release.

value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline across all timepoints
value.uncertainty: EQ-5D may have ceiling effects in this population; smaller effect sizes expected than condition-specific measures. Limited published data on MCID for Dupuytren.
value.rationale: Generic HRQoL measure shows modest gains after hand surgery. Fasciectomy may show slightly larger gains due to greater functional improvement. Both groups expected to show statistically significant but modest clinically important improvement.

value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline across all timepoints
value.uncertainty: Pain patterns differ: surgery causes immediate postoperative pain resolving over weeks; collagenase causes injection-related pain and bruising. Long-term pain reduction expected in both.
value.rationale: Successful contracture release reduces mechanical pain and improves function. Both treatments achieve this; surgery may have greater long-term pain reduction due to more complete release.

value.estimand: ITT population, measured at 3 weeks through 60 months
value.uncertainty: Satisfaction may vary by timepoint; early satisfaction favors less invasive collagenase, long-term may favor fasciectomy if recurrence occurs. No validated MCID for satisfaction VAS.
value.rationale: High satisfaction expected with both treatments. Minimally invasive approach initially preferred; durability concerns may affect long-term satisfaction particularly in collagenase group.

value.estimand: Safety population, any AE during 24 months post-treatment
value.uncertainty: Safety profiles differ: collagenase has more skin/subcutaneous AEs (edema, bruising, skin tears); surgery has surgical risks (nerve injury, infection, CRPS). Serious AEs rare with both.
value.rationale: Collagenase: expected skin reactions ~20-30%, serious events rare. Surgery: expected complications ~10-20% including nerve injury, infection, hematoma. Both treatments have acceptable safety in experienced hands.

value.estimand: Direct and indirect costs from baseline through 24 months
value.uncertainty: Cost data highly dependent on healthcare system and geographic setting. Indirect costs (sick leave) favor collagenase due to faster return to work. Recurrence requiring retreatment increases costs.
value.rationale: Multiple economic analyses demonstrate collagenase cost savings versus surgery due to outpatient administration, no operating room time, faster recovery. Difference persists even accounting for higher retreatment rates.

value.effect_measure: mean change in total active motion (degrees)
value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline at 3, 12, 24, 60 months
value.uncertainty: Total active motion correlates with extension deficit improvement. Recurrent disease may have limited gains due to joint stiffness or previous surgery.
value.rationale: Restoration of active motion primary goal of treatment. Fasciectomy achieves greater immediate correction; collagenase provides meaningful but slightly less improvement. Both clinically significant.

value.effect_measure: mean change in total active extension deficit (degrees)
value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline at 12, 24, 60 months
value.uncertainty: Long-term outcomes subject to recurrence. Durability favors surgery. Some regression expected in both groups over time, more pronounced with collagenase.
value.rationale: Extension deficit gains maintained better with surgery at longer follow-up. Collagenase group shows gradual recurrence; by 60 months difference may be substantial. Both maintain clinically meaningful improvement versus baseline.

value.estimand: ITT population, proportion with worsening at 60 months versus 3 months
value.uncertainty: Very long-term data limited. Recurrence accumulates over time; 60-month endpoint has high uncertainty. Predicted rates extrapolated from shorter-term studies.
value.rationale: Long-term recurrence expected higher with collagenase. By 5 years, substantial proportion of collagenase-treated patients may require further intervention. Fasciectomy maintains better durability.

value.effect_measure: mean change in palmar pain score
value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline across all timepoints
value.uncertainty: Palmar pain specific to Dupuytren disease less studied than general hand pain. Scar tissue from prior treatment may limit improvement. Some patients may have increased pain post-treatment.
value.rationale: Palmar pain expected to improve with successful treatment. Surgery may cause temporary increase in pain due to surgical scar. Long-term both groups show modest improvement or stabilization.

value.effect_measure: mean change in cold intolerance score
value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline across all timepoints
value.uncertainty: Cold intolerance associated with Dupuytren but not primary outcome in prior studies. Limited data on treatment effect. Surgery may improve vascularity; may also cause scarring affecting temperature regulation.
value.rationale: Cold intolerance may improve with better finger extension and circulation. Effect likely small and variable. Surgery may have greater effect due to tissue release and improved blood flow.

value.effect_measure: mean change in total passive extension deficit (degrees)
value.estimand: ITT population, change from baseline at 24 and 60 months
value.uncertainty: Passive extension typically improves more than active extension. Long-term durability concerns similar to active motion endpoints. Joint contracture may limit gains in recurrent disease.
value.rationale: Passive extension deficit closely tracks active deficit. Similar pattern expected with surgery achieving greater immediate and long-term correction. Both treatments provide clinically meaningful improvement.

analysis_trace: Trial NCT03406338 is a Phase 4 randomized controlled trial comparing surgical fasciectomy versus collagenase injection for recurrent Dupuytren disease. The trial enrolled 60 patients with 1:1 randomization. Primary endpoints assess extension deficit at 3 months and proportion with worsening at 24 months. Evidence base: Multiple systematic reviews and RCTs (2020-2025) demonstrate that both treatments effectively reduce contracture in primary Dupuytren disease, with collagenase showing non-inferiority to fasciectomy for short-term outcomes. However, recurrence rates are higher with collagenase. For recurrent disease specifically, evidence is limited but suggests collagenase remains effective as salvage therapy. Extension deficit improvements typically range 30-50 degrees with both treatments. QuickDASH scores improve 15-25 points. Safety profiles show collagenase has higher risk of skin reactions, edema, and bruising; fasciectomy carries surgical risks including nerve injury, infection, and CRPS. Cost analyses favor collagenase due to outpatient administration. Patient satisfaction generally favors less invasive approaches initially. Key uncertainty: This is the first RCT specifically in recurrent disease; prior evidence is primarily from primary disease or retrospective series. Expected completion September 2024 per protocol.

Evidence sources identified: PMID 33030553 (cost-effectiveness recurrent Dupuytren), PMID 39644138 (DISC trial collagenase vs fasciectomy UK), PMID 40834927 (cost-effectiveness analysis), PMID 39451139 (safety meta-analysis), PMID 33618538 (recurrent Dupuytren outcomes meta-analysis). All sources retrieved via Europe PMC search but full text not fetchable due to source restrictions. Evidence roles: indirect_direction for efficacy comparisons (primary disease data applied to recurrent), mechanism_background for safety profiles, indirect_direction for cost and patient-reported outcomes.

Population matching: Adult patients with recurrent Dupuytren contracture after prior fasciectomy, collagenase, or needle fasciotomy. Baseline extension deficit ≥30 degrees. Exclusions include prior trauma, >2 prior treatments, severe arthritis. This differs from primary disease trials where patients are treatment-naive, introducing uncertainty about treatment response in scarred tissue.

Treatment matching: Collagenase 0.8mg injection (Xiaflex) versus limited fasciectomy. Dose and administration consistent with approved labeling. Surgical technique per usual care allows for additional procedures (capsulotomy, skin graft) as needed.

Endpoint matching: Primary endpoint 0 (extension deficit change at 3 months) - directly comparable to prior RCTs. Primary endpoint 1 (worsening ≥20 degrees at 24 months) - novel endpoint for recurrence assessment; prior studies typically report recurrence proportion not worsening threshold. Secondary endpoints include QuickDASH, EQ-5D, pain, satisfaction, adverse events, costs, and range of motion - all standard for Dupuytren trials.

Key risks: 1) Higher recurrence with collagenase may lead to inferior long-term outcomes; 2) Recurrent disease may respond less well to both treatments due to tissue scarring; 3) Blinding challenges (gloves conceal scars but cannot blind treatment type completely); 4) Sample size 60 may be underpowered for secondary endpoints and subgroup analyses.
